paras: The threatened lynching of Robert Hardin was a pursuit in March 1888 of a young Black school teacher near Utica, Kentucky, by a posse or "lynching party" bent on lynching him. Hardin was accused of seducing his pupil Amanda Pry and other girls in his school and of causing Pry's death by an attempted abortion, and he fled before he could be arrested. No report in the coverage says the pursuers found him.

Hardin taught a colored school near Utica, a small village near Owensboro. Among his pupils was Amanda Pry, fifteen, the daughter of Henry Pry, described in an Owensboro dispatch as "a very wealthy colored farmer." According to that dispatch, the father questioned his daughter when he found something wrong, and she accused Hardin of seducing her and then trying to end the pregnancy.

Henry Pry was advised to have Hardin arrested and went to Owensboro to do so, but Hardin "took the alarm" and left "for parts unknown." An Evansville special instead said Hardin escaped only after the girl's death. Before she died, Pry was reported to have said that other girls in the school were also pregnant: five in the Evansville version, six aged thirteen to sixteen in the Owensboro version.

The Evansville special said a posse "was organized and will lynch him if found which will probably be before morning." The Owensboro dispatch said the case had "aroused that race to a frenzy" and that "A lynching party is now in hot pursuit of Hardin."
No report of Hardin's capture, an arrest or a trial was found in the coverage, which ends with a reprint on March 22.

The story ran only in white papers outside Kentucky, from Illinois to Dakota Territory, between March 9 and March 22. The earliest short item, carried by the Rock Island Daily Argus and the Washington Evening Star under an Owensboro dateline, reported the charge and Hardin's flight but no pursuit. The Argus version also told of a Miss Harlowe who died after childbirth and of John Van Maeter, who "skipped" with Hardin.

The Indiana State Sentinel headed its account "A Beastly School Teacher" and treated a lynching as the likely outcome. The longer dispatch, printed as "Peck's Bad Boy" by the Custer Chronicle and later The Frontier, called Hardin "the villian"; none of the papers commented on the planned lynching.
The reports differ on whether Pry was dead: the short Owensboro item said she "will die," while the Evansville and longer Owensboro reports said she died that day.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Hardin
bases: A posse or 'lynching party' was reported organized and in pursuit of Robert Hardin with the stated aim of lynching him, but no report says he was caught or harmed (A3, A4).

The pursuers' stated aim was to lynch Hardin over the girl's death, an extralegal punishment for an alleged crime (A3, A4), but no report in the coverage says he was found or killed, and no size of the party is given.

Two separately datelined reports, an Evansville special (A3) and an Owensboro dispatch (A4), agree that Hardin was accused, fled, and was pursued by a party intent on lynching him; two others confirm the accusation and flight (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Owensboro dispatch (short form)
accounts.gist: Hardin was charged with seducing nearly all the girls in his school and gave Pry medicine to produce an abortion; she 'will die' and he fled. No pursuit is mentioned.

accounts.label: Evansville special
accounts.gist: Pry died of an attempted abortion after naming Hardin and saying five other pupils were pregnant; Hardin escaped after her death and a posse was organized to lynch him if found.

accounts.label: Owensboro dispatch (long form)
accounts.gist: Hardin fled when Henry Pry went to Owensboro to have him arrested; the girl died after saying six other girls were pregnant and drugged; 'A lynching party is now in hot pursuit.'

framing.detail: The Sentinel's 'A Beastly School Teacher' blamed 'Hardin's lust' and reported the planned lynching as a likely outcome without comment.
The 'Peck's Bad Boy' dispatch called Hardin 'the villian' and said his crimes 'aroused that race to a frenzy', reporting the lynching party's pursuit without comment.
The Argus and the Evening Star ran the short Owensboro item on the accusation and flight only.
